posts.title: 700 PHP Packages Backdoored in 15 Minutes
posts.author: admin
posts.excerpt: Last Friday night, an attacker rewrote 700 versions of widely-used PHP packages in under fifteen minutes. Any developer who ran a routine dependency update during the hours that followed unknowingly handed over their AWS keys, GitHub tokens, SSH keys, and crypto wallet recovery phrases. This is what a software supply chain attack looks like in practice — and why your vendor's code is now your security problem.
posts.content:
Last Friday night, someone with push access to the Laravel-Lang GitHub organization rewrote every git tag across four widely-used PHP packages in under fifteen minutes. For the roughly fourteen hours that followed, any developer who ran composer install or composer update unknowingly had credential-stealing malware delivered to their machine. The packages — laravel-lang/lang, laravel-lang/attributes, laravel-lang/http-statuses, and laravel-lang/actions — are community-maintained localization libraries with millions of downloads and a long track record of being exactly the kind of boring, stable dependency nobody thinks twice about. That reputation is precisely what made them such a good target.

The attack mechanics are worth understanding, because they reveal something important about how supply chain attacks work. Rather than publishing a suspicious new version that might trigger automated alerts, the attacker rewrote the historical git tags — version 1.0, version 2.3, whatever — to point at newly malicious commits. When a developer pulled down what looked like a trusted, stable old release, they were getting a poisoned package that wired a helper file into PHP's autoloader, running it on every request the moment the package was installed. That helper reached out to a remote server and pulled down a Windows binary that went straight to work: AWS credentials, GitHub tokens, Stripe secrets, Kubernetes configs, SSH keys, .env files, crypto wallet recovery phrases — if it was on the developer's system and looked like a secret, it left.

Here is what makes this matter outside the world of PHP development: nobody on an affected team did anything wrong. No one clicked a phishing link. No one used a weak password. The malware arrived through the exact mechanism developers are supposed to use to manage their software. If your company runs any application built on Laravel, or if any of your vendors do, you may have been affected without a single person on your team making a mistake. Supply chain attacks are effective precisely because they weaponize trust. The attacker was not breaking in — they were walking through a door your security checklist never thought to lock.

The window of exposure ran from approximately 10:32 PM UTC on May 22 to midday on May 23. Any environment that ran composer operations during that period should be treated as compromised: rotate every credential you can identify, audit cloud access logs, and assume that anything stored in environment variables was exfiltrated. The packages themselves have since been restored, but credentials do not become safe just because the attack is over.

What this incident illustrates — again, for anyone keeping count — is that a strong perimeter does not protect you from a compromised supply chain. Firewalls, access controls, and security training are all necessary, but they share a blind spot: they assume the software itself is trustworthy. Auditing your software supply chain, understanding where your dependencies come from, and knowing whether you would detect a tampering event before it costs you — these are genuinely hard problems, and they require specialized expertise that most organizations do not have in-house. The teams that get caught in attacks like this are, almost without exception, the ones who believed that was someone else's job.
